title: Bolt.new Pricing 2026: Free Tier, Pro Plans & Token Limits Explained
description: Complete Bolt.new pricing breakdown for 2026 — what the free tier actually gives you, Pro plan costs, token limits, and whether it's worth paying for vs alternatives like v0 or Lovable.
content:
## How Bolt.new pricing works

Bolt.new charges by token consumption. Every AI action — generating code, editing a file, running a command — burns tokens from your monthly allowance.

| Plan | Price | Tokens/month |
|---|---|---|
| Free | $0 | ~150K |
| Pro | $20/month | 10M |
| Teams | $30/user/month | 10M/user |
| Enterprise | Custom | Custom |

## What tokens actually cost you

Tokens map loosely to words processed by the model. Rough estimates:

- "Add a button to this page" = 2,000-5,000 tokens
- "Build a full authentication system" = 50,000-200,000 tokens
- A complete small app from scratch = 500,000-2M tokens

The 150K free allowance runs out fast on anything beyond a quick demo. It's enough to evaluate the product; it's not enough to build something real.

## Pro at $20/month

10M tokens covers serious daily use — iterating on multiple projects, deploying real applications. Beyond token volume, Pro adds priority queue access, newer model access as they're released, and full deployment through Netlify and other providers.

At $20/month it's the same price as GitHub Copilot and Cursor, so the comparison is worth making.

## What Bolt.new can build

Full-stack web applications generated and run in the browser — React, Next.js, Vue, Svelte, Astro, Node.js backends, Supabase databases. Deploys to Netlify or Cloudflare Pages.

The in-browser execution environment is the actual differentiator. You can run, preview, and deploy without touching your local machine. Useful for demos and quick MVPs; less suited to serious production codebases.

## How it compares

| | Bolt.new | v0 (Vercel) | Lovable | Cursor |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Price | $20/mo | $20/mo | $25/mo | $20/mo |
| Approach | Full-stack in browser | React UI components | Full-stack + Supabase | IDE-first |
| Best for | Quick app prototypes | UI/component generation | Startup MVPs | Daily coding |

Bolt.new makes sense for prototyping where you want something live fast without setting up a local environment. Cursor is the better choice once you have an existing codebase to work with. v0 is worth looking at if you specifically need high-quality React UI output.

## Worth $20/month?

For regular prototyping and MVP work, probably yes — the time saved on environment setup is real. For production codebases as your primary coding tool, probably not. Generated code quality is decent but inconsistent on large applications, and context limitations become visible as projects grow.

title: CircleCI Review 2026: Is It Still the Best CI/CD Platform?
description: Honest CircleCI review for 2026 — features, pricing, AI capabilities, free tier limits, and how it compares to GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, and Jenkins.
content:
## CircleCI in 2026

CircleCI was the CI/CD default before GitHub Actions captured most of the market. It's still a solid platform — for specific use cases, test parallelism especially, it's hard to beat. But for GitHub-native teams with straightforward pipelines, the case for paying for CircleCI has gotten thinner every year.

## Pricing

| Plan | Price | Credits/month |
|---|---|---|
| Free | $0 | 6,000 (~60 min) |
| Performance | From $15/month | 25,000+ |
| Scale | Custom | Unlimited |
| Server (self-hosted) | Custom | Unlimited |

CircleCI bills in compute credits. 1,000 credits = 10 minutes on a medium Linux machine. The free tier's 6,000 credits is about 60 minutes per month — enough to test the platform, not enough for a real team. GitHub Actions gives 2,000 free minutes by comparison.

Docker Layer Caching costs 200 credits per job run on top of base compute. At 500 runs/month that adds $60/month in DLC charges alone. Run the numbers before committing.

## Where it earns its reputation

Test splitting is the standout feature. CircleCI analyzes historical test run times and distributes your suite across parallel containers to minimize wall-clock time. For large test suites this routinely cuts build times by 50-70%. GitHub Actions has no equivalent built in.

SSH debugging is the other practical differentiator. You can SSH into a failed build container and poke around interactively. When a pipeline is failing for non-obvious reasons, this is substantially faster than adding print statements and re-running.

The Orb ecosystem provides reusable, pre-configured integrations for common tasks — deploying to AWS, running Cypress, publishing packages. Not as large as GitHub Actions' marketplace, but well-maintained.

## The honest case against it

The free tier is too stingy to evaluate properly. 60 minutes per month means most teams hit limits immediately and face a buying decision before they've validated fit.

Credit-based billing is hard to forecast. Usage spikes during release cycles, and the bill follows. Teams with variable CI usage often find flat-rate alternatives easier to budget.

For teams already on GitHub Actions, the switching cost is real. The YAML syntax differs, the mental model differs, and integrations need to be rebuilt.

## Who it's for

CircleCI makes sense when test suite speed is a real bottleneck, when you're not tied to GitHub and want a mature hosted CI platform, or when you need self-hosted CI with full feature parity to the cloud product. It doesn't make sense as a GitHub Actions replacement unless you have specific pain points that CircleCI solves better.

title: Best Snyk Alternatives in 2026: Free & Paid Developer Security Tools
description: The best alternatives to Snyk in 2026 — Semgrep, Socket.dev, Aikido Security, Jit.io, and SonarQube compared on features, pricing, and use case fit.
content:
## Snyk alternatives worth knowing

Teams move away from Snyk for a few consistent reasons: free tier scan limits get hit quickly in CI/CD, the Team plan at $25/user/month becomes expensive for larger teams, and some teams need SAST capabilities that Snyk Code doesn't fully cover.

## Semgrep — best for custom rules

[Semgrep](/tools/semgrep/) is open source static analysis with a pattern-matching language that lets you write your own security rules. Snyk Code gives you pre-built rules you can't modify. Semgrep gives you a rule engine you control.

If your security team has internal coding standards, proprietary patterns, or specific compliance requirements to enforce, Semgrep handles what Snyk can't. The open source version has no scan limits and 2,000+ community rules to start from.

The tradeoff: Semgrep requires more configuration. Snyk is closer to plug-and-play; Semgrep requires someone to own the rule library.

## Socket.dev — best for supply chain threats

[Socket.dev](/tools/socket-dev/) analyzes package behavior rather than checking CVEs. It detects packages that contain malicious code, typosquat on popular libraries, or make unusual network calls — the category of threats that CVE databases don't capture because they're not disclosed vulnerabilities.

This makes Socket a complement to Snyk rather than a replacement. If supply chain security is a priority, Socket catches what Snyk misses. It has a GitHub PR integration and a useful free tier.

## Aikido Security — best all-in-one for smaller teams

[Aikido Security](/tools/aikido-security/) covers the same ground as Snyk — SAST, SCA, containers, IaC, secrets — at a more competitive price point for small and mid-size teams. The interface is less cluttered, and the deduplication engine handles false positives more aggressively than Snyk does out of the box.

The tradeoff is a smaller community and ecosystem. If you need a broad set of existing integrations, Snyk wins on that dimension.

## Jit.io — best for teams with existing tools

[Jit.io](/tools/jit-io/) orchestrates open source security tools — Semgrep, Trivy, Gitleaks, and others — under a single interface with unified policy management and CI/CD integration. Instead of replacing your tools, it coordinates them.

If you're already using Semgrep for SAST, Trivy for container scanning, and Gitleaks for secrets, Jit gives you a single view without paying for Snyk on top. The free tier covers small teams.

## SonarQube — best for code quality plus security

[SonarQube](/tools/sonarqube/) covers both code quality (complexity, maintainability, test coverage) and security vulnerabilities. The Community Edition is free and self-hosted.

For teams that care about code hygiene as much as security, SonarQube's combined analysis provides more value than Snyk Code alone. Quality gates can block PRs that don't meet thresholds on either dimension. The tradeoff: self-hosting requires infrastructure, and the UI is less polished than Snyk's.

## Quick comparison

| Tool | Best for | Free tier | Open source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Semgrep | Custom SAST rules | Unlimited | Yes |
| Socket.dev | Supply chain security | Yes | No |
| Aikido | All-in-one, lower cost | Yes | No |
| Jit.io | Orchestrating OSS tools | Yes | No |
| SonarQube | Quality + security | Self-hosted | Yes |

title: PagerDuty Review 2026: Features, Pricing & Best Alternatives
description: Full PagerDuty review for 2026 — on-call scheduling, incident response, AIOps features, pricing tiers, and whether it's still worth it vs Opsgenie, Grafana IRM, or incident.io.
content:
## PagerDuty

PagerDuty connects your monitoring stack to your on-call engineers. Alerts come in from Datadog, Grafana, CloudWatch, or wherever else, and PagerDuty routes them to the right person based on schedule, escalation policy, and service ownership. In 2026, it has added AIOps capabilities: noise reduction, automated triage, and AI-generated incident summaries.

## Pricing

| Plan | Price | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Free | $0 (up to 5 users) | Basic on-call, limited integrations |
| Professional | $21/user/month | Full on-call, escalation, analytics |
| Business | $41/user/month | Postmortems, stakeholder updates, event intelligence |
| Enterprise | Custom | AIOps, full automation, SSO |

The free tier's 5-user limit means most teams hit a paywall before they've properly evaluated it. Professional at $21/user/month is where PagerDuty actually becomes useful — a 10-person on-call team is $210/month, a 50-person team is $1,050/month. It scales linearly and gets expensive.

The AIOps features (ML-based alert grouping, automated noise reduction) are on Business and Enterprise. You're paying extra for what's become the main reason to choose PagerDuty over cheaper alternatives.

## What it does well

On-call scheduling is mature. Multi-layer escalation policies, business-hours vs after-hours routing, overrides, and rotation management. Teams with complex on-call structures — multiple tiers, different pools for different services — find PagerDuty handles edge cases that simpler tools don't.

Alert grouping reduces noise. PagerDuty's event intelligence correlates related alerts into a single incident, cutting down on duplicate pages. For teams running noisy monitoring environments, this is the feature that justifies the cost.

Automation Actions can run predefined runbooks when incidents hit certain criteria — restart a service, scale a deployment, clear a cache — without waking anyone. This is PagerDuty's closest answer to automated remediation.

## The honest caveats

PagerDuty doesn't reduce alert volume. It routes it better and groups it intelligently, but the underlying noise problem in your monitoring still exists. Teams that mute their PagerDuty channel by month three haven't solved anything — they've confirmed the alerting setup needs fixing first.

The UI has accumulated complexity over years of feature additions. New users often find it overwhelming. Newer tools like incident.io have cleaner interfaces for teams that don't need every feature PagerDuty offers.

## How it compares

| | PagerDuty | Opsgenie | Grafana IRM | incident.io |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Price | $21/user/mo | $9/user/mo | Freemium | $16/user/mo |
| Best for | Enterprise depth | Cost-conscious teams | Grafana stack | Modern UX |
| On-call scheduling | Best in class | Strong | Good | Good |

Opsgenie covers the core use case at less than half the price — choose it if budget is the primary constraint. Grafana IRM makes sense if you're already running Grafana for observability. incident.io is worth evaluating for teams that want cleaner UX and structured postmortem workflows.

title: DevOps Pipelines Guide 2026: CI/CD Tools, Best Practices & How to Choose
description: Complete guide to DevOps pipelines in 2026 — what a CI/CD pipeline does, the best tools (GitHub Actions, Azure Pipelines, GitLab CI, CircleCI, Jenkins), and how to pick the right one for your team.
content:
## DevOps pipelines in 2026

A CI/CD pipeline automates the path from code commit to production deployment. The basic shape is consistent across tools: trigger on a push or PR, build the code, run tests, package an artifact, deploy to staging, deploy to production, verify it's still up.

The goal is catching problems before they reach users and shipping changes frequently enough that each individual release is low risk.

## The main platforms

GitHub Actions is the default for most teams. It's native to GitHub, has 2,000 free minutes/month for private repos, and a marketplace with 15,000+ pre-built actions. For teams already on GitHub with no unusual requirements, there's no strong reason to look elsewhere.

Azure DevOps Pipelines is the right call for Microsoft-stack teams — .NET, Azure deployments, Windows build agents. It offers 1,800 free minutes/month and native GitHub Copilot integration for pipeline authoring. If your team has Copilot licenses, AI assistance in pipeline configuration is included at no extra cost.

GitLab CI/CD is part of the broader GitLab platform — source control, CI/CD, security scanning, and deployment under one roof. For teams that want a single vendor across the whole DevOps lifecycle, or for on-premises and air-gapped deployments, it's the most integrated option.

CircleCI is still the best platform for test parallelism. Its AI-powered test splitting distributes your test suite across parallel containers based on historical run times, which can cut build times significantly on large test suites. The free tier is stingy — about 60 minutes/month — so budget for the paid tier if you go this route.

Jenkins is self-hosted, open source, and infinitely customizable. It has a plugin for everything. It also has maintenance overhead, slower setup, and a steeper learning curve than hosted platforms. The right choice for teams with genuinely unusual pipeline requirements or strict infrastructure control needs.

## What to evaluate

Parallelism matters more than most teams realize. How many jobs can run simultaneously? What does the free tier actually allow?

Caching is the single biggest lever for build speed. A pipeline that reinstalls node_modules from scratch every run is leaving minutes on the table.

Self-hosted runners are necessary for GPU builds, Windows-specific workflows, or teams with data residency requirements. Most platforms support them; the terms and pricing vary.

Secrets management details matter for security posture. Most platforms handle this reasonably — worth checking before you're deep into a migration.

## Platform comparison

| Platform | Free tier | Self-hosted | Best for |
|---|---|---|---|
| GitHub Actions | 2,000 min/mo | Yes | GitHub teams |
| Azure Pipelines | 1,800 min/mo | Yes | Microsoft/Azure stack |
| GitLab CI | 400 min/mo | Yes | All-in-one DevOps |
| CircleCI | ~60 min/mo | Yes | Test parallelism |
| Jenkins | Unlimited | Always | Custom workflows |

## How to decide

On GitHub with no particular pain points: GitHub Actions. On Azure or .NET: Azure Pipelines. Want everything under one vendor: GitLab. Test suite is the bottleneck: CircleCI. Need full control over build infrastructure: Jenkins, and accept the maintenance cost.
